article.articleHeadline: Contracting Influenza A: Indiscriminate Use of Tamiflu Can Be Harmful.
article.articleSummary:
- Influenza A management in Vietnam cautions against indiscriminate use of oseltamivir (Tamiflu). Most influenza A infections are mild and resolve in about a week, but severe disease and complications can occur, especially in high-risk groups: children under 5 (especially under 2), adults 65+, and those with cardiovascular disease, asthma, COPD, diabetes, liver or kidney disease, or neurological conditions. Immunocompromised individuals (cancer treatment, organ transplantation, HIV, long-term immunosuppression) and pregnant women or up to two weeks postpartum are at higher risk. Obesity (BMI ≥40), under-19 on long-term aspirin, and residents of long-term care facilities also require evaluation. Tamiflu should be considered early for severe cases or high-risk patients, ideally within 48 hours
- Influenza A in children, particularly A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) circulating in Vietnam, usually presents with sudden high fever, cough, runny nose, sore throat, and fatigue; vomiting or diarrhea may occur. Most recover within about a week, though cough can persist beyond two weeks, and severe complications can occur in young children or those with underlying conditions. Doctors Bùi Hoàng Vinh and Nguyễn Thị Huyên of Bệnh viện Quân y 175 advise parents to monitor respiratory effort, consciousness, and feeding. Five warning signs require immediate medical care: 1) fast/abnormal breathing; 2) persistent high fever (≥39°C) not responding to antipyretics or febrile seizures; 3) chest or severe muscle pain; 4) cyanosis or cold extremities; 5) lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, or dehydration. article.articleHeadline: The RFI Club - RFI Club Butembo (DRC): an awareness campaign to contain the Ebola outbreak.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak containment in Butembo, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is supported by volunteers from the RFI Club Butembo, who launch STOP Ebola awareness campaigns in regional schools to promote preventive measures against the virus. The initiative emphasizes education and community engagement to curb transmission. Kizito Makélélé, president of the RFI Butembo club, participates, with sociologist Francis Sterling Mongbe as guest. As of 1 November 2026, the report highlights local, school-based outreach as part of outbreak containment efforts for Ebola in the region.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Kisangani hosts the intra-action review to improve the response.
article.articleSummary: Kisangani hosted a three-day intra-action review (RIA) from Oct 29–31, 2026, on the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus disease (EVD), the 17th outbreak. The exercise aimed to capitalize on lessons learned and set priorities to boost coordination and response speed. Delegates from Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Ituri analyzed field interventions under the theme: Together, learn from the response to protect communities and save lives. In Haut-Uele, Governor Jean Bakomito Gambu highlighted measures and the Cadenas operation to curb spread, plus province-financed logistics: 3 ambulances, 2 hearses, 30+ motorcycles across seven health zones, and 13 motorized tricycles. Challenges cited included community resistance, mining-area vulnerability, vehicle shortages, delayed payments, and weak capacity at Dungu, Rungu, Niangara and Wamba hospitals. Recommendations call for strengthened surveillance, better medical care, and intensified community engagement. The Director of Cabinet closed the session, urging rapid action toward eradicating the outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Kasindi: collaboration between Congolese and Ugandan communities encouraged - ACP.
article.articleSummary: Ebola Virus Disease has appeared in Kasindi, a border town with Uganda in North Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo. Following the first reported case, Congolese and Ugandan communities are urged to collaborate, as Ebola crosses borders. Civil society leader Paul Zaidi emphasizes solidarity and warns that the outbreak is not insurmountable when prevention measures are observed and health workers are supported. In Kasindi-Lubiriha, within Mutwanga health zone, 20 confirmed Ebola cases and 12 deaths had been recorded as of 26 October 2026. Community mobilization through Risk Communication and Community Engagement (Crec), surveillance, testing, and patient care are acknowledged. Measures promoted include proper handwashing with clean water and soap or hydroalcoholic gel, rapid reporting of suspected cases, and working with health teams to control transmission. Authorities hope joint efforts will contain spread and allow cross-border activities to resume safely.

At M'Poko Bac landing site near Bangui, travellers from the DRC undergo handwashing, temperature checks and personal-detail registration as part of enhanced surveillance. Authorities cite the virus in three DRC border regions along a 1,500-km frontier and ongoing river traffic, which sustains cross-border movement. Despite tighter controls, river-based livelihoods persist. TV5 Monde notes over 10,000 EVD cases in Africa, most in the DRC, with additional cases in Kenya and Nigeria. article.articleHeadline: A nurse showed how she put on the full protective equipment before entering the Ebola unit's high-risk area.
article.articleSummary: Outbreak of Bundibugyo ebolavirus declared in May in northeast Democratic Republic of the Congo; transmission via direct contact with bodily fluids of infected or deceased individuals. Nurse Laura Lampe demonstrated, per World Health Organization PPE protocol, how to don full protective equipment before entering the Ebola treatment unit's high-risk area. Preparation started with rubber boots and gloves, followed by tear checks, a colleague zipping the suit, then an N95 mask, goggles, hood, and double gloves. She annotated her back with her name, profession, and unit entry time. The demonstration underscores the critical role of step-by-step protective gear in safeguarding health workers in high-risk zones amid the ongoing outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Nakuru enlists medics who worked in West Africa virus outbreak
article.articleSummary: Kenya reports nine confirmed Ebola virus disease cases, including two deaths, after an imported case on Oct 6, 2026, traced from the DRC via Uganda to Nairobi; eight secondary cases involve relatives or healthcare workers with close contact to the index patient. Nakuru County has enlisted health workers who fought the 2014–2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak and the Covid-19 response to handle suspected cases in the Northern Corridor. Eight urban centres along the corridor—Mai Mahiu, Longonot, Naivasha, Gilgil, Kikopey, Pipeline and Salgaa—are identified as high‑risk transit hubs for potential transmission. Nakuru has designated Ebola isolation centres at Langalanga and Naivasha hospitals and conducted a training and simulation exercise with MoH trainers and Amref Health Africa in Kenya, covering screening, PPE, safe transport, and laboratory testing. Rapid Response Teams and community sensitization are active.

article.articleHeadline: A man with monkeypox was hospitalized in Domodedovo.
article.articleSummary: Monkeypox patient, a 38-year-old man, hospitalized at Domodedovo Central Hospital, Moscow Oblast, with confirmed monkeypox. Disease can include fever, lymphadenopathy, and a characteristic rash, with transmission through close contact with an infected person or animal.

article.articleHeadline: Kenya seeks churches' help to curb Ebola
article.articleSummary: Kenya reported nine Ebola cases of the Bundibugyo strain by late October, with two deaths and no community transmission. The government appealed to faith communities to back prevention efforts as churches adopt Covid-era tactics to curb spread, dispel rumours, and encourage early reporting. Priests and faith leaders were urged to weave health messages into sermons and programs; churches have already promoted handwashing, stigma reduction, and safe burial guidance. Faith groups demand greater government transparency, enhanced surveillance, and preparedness, including ready quarantine and treatment centres. In June, the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops opposed a quarantine facility at Nanyuki airbase over concerns about foreigners. The first Kenyan case travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo; the second death was a 65-year-old relative, with seven others in isolation. Nigeria reported one Bundibugyo case in Abuja (Uganda-born wife of a Swiss diplomat); DRC’s outbreak toll stood at 4,700 deaths from 9,700 cases across eight provinces.

article.articleHeadline: Ituri: the lack of water undermines Ebola prevention at the ISP displaced persons site in Bunia.
article.articleSummary: At the ISP displaced persons site in Bunia, Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ebola prevention is undermined by a lack of potable water and missing handwashing stations. Olivier Bavi Karba, president of the Ituri IDP Association (ADPI), says water access problems and the absence of handwashing facilities erode hygiene practices, raising Ebola transmission risk among a vulnerable population living in precarious conditions. He calls on residents to sustain barrier measures and follow health recommendations, including precautions during movement to host quarters, and to extend vigilance to host communities to prevent spillover. The World Health Organization warned in June that displacement, overcrowding, and inadequate WASH services hinder early case detection and prevention of Ebola, complicating response at IDP sites. Restoring handwashing setups, ensuring constant water and soap, and boosting community awareness are essential to improve prevention at the ISP as the Ebola outbreak persists in Ituri.

article.articleHeadline: The threat posed by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) to children.
article.articleSummary: As of early October 2026, the Respiratory Department at Nghệ An Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital in Vietnam reports increased RSV infections in children compared with the same period in 2025, including severe cases. RSV commonly causes upper respiratory illness in children under 2 and can progress to bronchiolitis or pneumonia, with seasonality peaking in winter–spring. Symptoms include runny nose, congestion, cough, fever, poor feeding, and fatigue; severe disease may involve fast breathing, wheeze, chest indrawing, lethargy, or apnea. High-risk groups include infants under 6 months, premature babies, and those with congenital heart or lung disease. Immunity is not long-lasting, so reinfection is possible. Monoclonal antibodies are used for prevention in selected children after clinician assessment. Preventive measures: hand hygiene, surface cleaning, avoiding contact with ill individuals, avoiding tobacco smoke, and ventilated spaces. Seek medical care for breathing difficulty or persistent fever; do not self-medicate.

article.articleHeadline: Ho Chi Minh City strengthens dengue fever and hand-foot-and-mouth disease prevention.
article.articleSummary: Surveillance data for weeks 41–43 show Con Dao Special Administrative Zone among localities with high dengue fever and hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) incidence in Ho Chi Minh City, alongside Ngai Giao and Minh Thanh communes and Can Gio. Citywide weekly dengue cases ranged 1,603–1,785; HFMD 1,800–1,850. By week 43 (19–25 Oct 2026), cumulative totals reached 42,515 dengue and 44,191 HFMD cases, with 11 dengue and 5 HFMD deaths. Response tasks mandate simultaneous, disease-specific prevention: dengue vector control with environmental cleanup, removal of standing water, larviciding, and spraying only per professional guidelines; HFMD emphasis on nurseries, kindergartens, schools, and households—maintaining hygiene, disinfection, health monitoring, and timely reporting to health stations. A citywide high-profile campaign includes Dĩ An ward and the University of Ho Chi Minh City dormitory complex (500+ students). Authorities stress early detection and proactive risk elimination to prevent resurgence.

article.articleHeadline: Germs on a plane
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-11-01, the article notes that during Jan 2021–Sept 2022 Australia mandated masks on domestic and inbound flights, a rule ended in Sept 2022; masks are now rare at Australian airports, while in South-East Asia masking remains common in airports. Anecdotes describe recent colds and flu after flying to Singapore and Bali; similar infections on travel. A 2018 Boeing-funded study found sitting in the same row as a sick passenger carries about 80% infection risk; seats directly across aisle have 10–30% risk; other cabin positions carry under 3% baseline risk. A Helsinki Airport study same year found about 10% of surfaces harbor viruses such as rhinovirus; trays were the most germy, toilets least. Masks help by reducing touching nose/mouth; handwashing and sanitizer also help. Global air travel rebounds to above pre-pandemic levels and may double in 20 years; the article argues masks remain a prudent defense.

article.articleHeadline: Yogyakarta Becomes Benchmark for Wolbachia Development, Dengue Cases 76 Percent Lower.
article.articleSummary: Yogyakarta has become a benchmark for Wolbachia-based dengue control in Indonesia. Five years after comprehensive Wolbachia deployment, dengue incidence in Yogyakarta was 76% lower than in Java cities without Wolbachia intervention. Monitoring 2023–2024 showed Wolbachia in Aedes aegypti reached 89%. The findings underpin the SHIELD project (Scaling Health Interventions for Effective Long-term Dengue Control), led by Universitas Gadjah Mada’s Center for Tropical Medicine, which launched its kickoff on 22 October 2026. SHIELD aims to learn from Wolbachia implementation in five Indonesian cities to inform strategies for broader rollout, nationally and globally, through four working groups: Implementation Research, Entomology, Epidemiology, and Modeling. Monash University researcher Katie Anders notes the impact persisted up to seven years post-release. The study cautions that Wolbachia reduces but does not eliminate dengue and must be integrated with other control measures.

IDI West Java chief Dr. Moch Lutfhi cautioned against jumping to conclusions, noting that mass gastroenteritis (muntaber) can result from viral infections, bacterial infections such as Salmonella or Escherichia coli, or contaminated food and beverages. No definitive link to food poisoning or a specific virus has been established pending further epidemiological investigation by the Health Department. Investigators will assess whether travelers shared meals or drinks, the onset timing of symptoms, and possible person-to-person transmission. In the meantime, treatment prioritizes preventing dehydration with oral rehydration solutions or intravenous fluids. For mild cases, gradual but frequent oral rehydration is advised to avoid fluid and electrolyte loss.

article.articleHeadline: At the Edge of a Palm Oil Plantation, Researchers Found a Mosquito Carrying the DNA of the Monkey Malaria Parasite.
article.articleSummary: In Langkat Regency, North Sumatra, Indonesia, researchers studied two villages in Desa Ujung Bandar, Salapian district, amid palm-oil plantations and disturbed forests. From July 2022 to June 2023, four nightly human landing catches (18:30–06:00) yielded 597 mosquitoes: 584 were Anopheles dirus and 13 Anopheles scanloni. DNA testing found six An. dirus carrying malaria parasite DNA, including Plasmodium knowlesi in three specimens (about 0.5% of those tested) and Plasmodium vivax in four; all An. scanloni tested were parasite-free. This provides the first evidence of An. dirus and An. scanloni in Sumatra and suggests An. dirus as a potential vector for knowlesi malaria there, though DNA presence does not prove transmission. The finding expands knowlesi’s distribution beyond prior sites and highlights the need for further ecological and entomological studies on vector behavior in Sumatra, where North Sumatra reported 377 knowlesi cases in 2017.

article.articleHeadline: Can bacteria and viruses within three meters of a neck-worn device be wiped out in one fell swoop? CCTV exposes the truth about air disinfection cards.
article.articleSummary: China’s CCTV report exposes 'air disinfection cards' worn around the neck claiming to sterilize bacteria and viruses within three meters. Sold online for a few tenths to tens of yuan per card, some labeled overseas, each with about 60 days of use and marketed as safe for children. They allegedly release chlorine dioxide to form an 'isolation protection layer' around the wearer, with third-party testing claiming >99.99% kill against Influenza A virus in a 1 m^3 chamber. The China Consumers Association filed public-interest lawsuits against Shunfeng Gene Technology (Weifang), Zhongcheng Northern Biomed (Shenyang), and Qingdao Zhongke Ruiye Gene Biotech (Qingdao). Shandong High Court upheld punitive damages: Shunfeng 2 million yuan; the other two jointly 1.06 million yuan. Experts say chlorine dioxide is a strong oxidizer; safe levels do not disinfect. Per-card content is 3–15 g. Public urged to rely on hygiene-safety-evaluated products checked on the national site.

article.articleHeadline: ScienceNet - The Fifth Seminar on Eradication of Vertically Transmitted Poultry Diseases Convened
article.articleSummary: The Fifth Seminar on Eradication of Vertically Transmitted Poultry Diseases convened in Xinxing County, Yunfu City, Guangdong Province, China, on 2026-11-01, with over 230 industry representatives from 18 provinces. The theme centered on deepening source purification, biosafety, and triggering purification across poultry production. Key speakers outlined comprehensive strategies: Wang Hongning (CAE, Sichuan University) proposed six-precision measures—accurate detection, tracing, disinfection, immunization, purification, and targeted drug use—to strengthen source governance within a biosafety framework. Zhao Guiping (National Broiler Industry Technology System) urged anti-disease breeding, domestically produced diagnostic reagents, and broad-spectrum vaccines to reinforce source security. Zhang Xiaorong emphasized Mycoplasma control and purification as a cornerstone of green poultry farming, advocating case-specific strategies. Additional topics covered phage-therapy applications for Salmonella purification, diagnostics for major vertically transmitted pathogens, and vector-borne risk management. Attendees visited Wens Institute to review intelligent storage, research platforms, and detection workflows, followed by a focused technical Q&A session.

article.articleHeadline: A new coronavirus variant with many mutations... does it herald a new wave of infections?
article.articleSummary: PJ.2.1, a coronavirus variant detected in May 2026, is circulating in Canada, the United States, and Europe. Scientists largely contest that it signals a new wave of infections. Dr. Albert Rezanov of Kazan Federal University notes that highly mutated lineages like BA.2.86 (Pirola) have appeared in immunocompromised patients, where prolonged infection fosters rapid change; more mutations do not necessarily mean higher virulence or faster spread. A German study finds PJ.2.1 markedly distinct from prior strains, with multiple spike protein mutations, and it predominantly affects people aged 60 and above; Chinese researchers nickname it “the Jump” due to extensive changes. The variant shows high affinity for the ACE2 receptor but does not yet evade immunity, though its binding could permit rapid accumulation of mutations that might enable future immune escape. No evidence yet of an imminent outbreak.

Young and high‑risk individuals may develop severe disease, including throat edema and pneumonia, if treatment is delayed. Antigen tests can be negative early; clinical judgment is essential. Antivirals are most effective within 48 hours but remain beneficial beyond that window for high‑risk patients. Vaccination is advisable; protection develops in 2–4 weeks, with a winter–spring peak (December–March), and it’s not too late to vaccinate.

The inexigibilidade de licitação contract, signed in October last year by then Health Secretary Rubem Bottas, covers 100,000 books at R$29.90 each. The City transferred about R$1.49 million to the supplier, Ecomais Distribuidora de Materiais Didáticos e Sistemas de Ensino Educacionais, based in Rio Preto. A February warehouse fire destroyed 39,700 kits. The representation argues lack of competition and no unique technical feature, noting the QR Code materials are widely available. In April, the municipality said students received the books and some units were distributed to health facilities. The City states the Procuradoria-Geral do Município will review the points, and, after technical input from the Education Department, will present justifications within the legal timeline.

article.articleHeadline: Diarrheal diseases record 6 million cases in Brazil; learn how to prevent | Roraima in Focus
article.articleSummary: Brazil recorded over 6 million cases of acute diarrheal diseases (ADD) from January to October 2026, according to the Health Ministry's dashboard. Transmission is fecal-oral, driven by norovirus and rotavirus, plus bacteria and parasites. Young children, especially infants, and the elderly are most at risk, particularly where water, sanitation, or food storage is poor. Prevention emphasizes hand hygiene, avoiding cross-contamination, proper cooking, refrigeration, and using safe water. If water is not potable, filter or strain and boil for five minutes after boiling begins; or disinfect with two drops of 2.5% sodium hypochlorite per liter and wait 30 minutes. Do not reuse the same knife or cutting board for raw and ready-to-eat foods; avoid washing poultry in sinks. Symptoms include three or more diarrheal episodes in 24 hours, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever; blood or mucus may appear. Stool testing and PCR panels aid diagnosis; dehydration is the main complication—seek care if concerned.

article.articleHeadline: 'Super-virus' warning issued to thousands of Scots at risk of grim flu strain
article.articleSummary: Scotland faces warnings that a viral mutation could create a deadly influenza strain by co-infection of animal and human flu in people with close livestock contact. The alert follows a Brazilian woman's death from swine flu and reports of avian flu illnesses in China and Cambodia, though health authorities say animal-origin flu does not usually spread person-to-person. article.articleHeadline: Heartworm appears in dogs from Foz, but is not on official records.
article.articleSummary: Heartworm disease (Dirofilaria immitis) detected in dogs in Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil, suggesting possible local transmission. Official municipal records show zero canine dirofilariasis cases since January 2020, as the disease is not a notifiable condition and routine reporting is absent. Local veterinarians report regular diagnoses, including at least one case per year at Hospital Veterinário Popvet since 2020; some dogs reportedly never left Foz, implying local exposure, though authorities caution that history alone cannot confirm transmission. Diagnostic workflows often start with a rapid multi-disease test (Anaplasma, ehrlichiosis, Lyme, and dirofilariasis) that can flag dirofilariasis; confirmation relies on echocardiography showing adult worms and sometimes microfilaremia on blood smear. The Aedes aegypti mosquito is a potential vector; municipal surveillance focuses on dengue. Case example: border collie Zoe coughing in late 2025, diagnosed via echocardiography in Foz. As of 1 Nov 2026, prevalence data remain incomplete.

article.articleHeadline: Meningitis: Test incorporated into SUS may yield a result in one hour - Folha Vitória
article.articleSummary: Multiplex PCR testing of cerebrospinal fluid for meningitis and encephalitis enables results in about one hour, improving management in Brazil. The test detects 14 pathogens across bacteria, viruses, and fungi, with sensitivity around 94.2% and specificity 99.8%. It complements culture, not replacing it entirely. In SUS, CONITEC Recommendation 938 (Nov 2024) favored incorporation; it became mandatory 180 days after publication and is in force. In private health plans, ANS Resolution 627 (Feb 17, 2025) added coverage for 'Agents Infectious in Encephalitis and Meningitis - Detection by PCR multiplex in CSF.' Economic analyses project hospitalization reductions: about 1 day less for the general population and 2 days for pediatric patients, and shorter empirical therapy by roughly 12 days (general) and 4 days (children). Example panel targets include Escherichia coli K1 and Haemophilus (influenzae).

article.articleHeadline: Brazil Ebola Form for São Paulo and Rio Flights Nov 3

The rule applies to all departures from Brazil and through flights; return trips that week may be covered; a stop in the US counts. Signing: any passenger over 18 or an authorized adult; one adult can attest for a whole party; signatures may be paper, digital, electronic checkbox, or verbal attestation with a recorded record. Languages: Spanish/French versions anticipated; Portuguese version not announced. The official microbiological report nº 48826/2026, cited in Resolution RE 4.227/2026 (26 October 2026), showed contamination contravening sanitary legislation. Zanetti initiated a voluntary recall; Anvisa also halted manufacturing, marketing, distribution, advertising, and use of the affected lot. Listeria monocytogenes can cause listeriosis, posing higher risk to pregnant women, newborns, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. The RDC 655/2022 framework requires mandatory recall when a product poses health risks, with notification to Anvisa within 48 hours. Consumers who bought the sausage should check lot 21/08/2026 and avoid consumption; the measure targets only the specified lot, not the entire brand.

article.articleHeadline: Leishmaniasis: A disease humanity has never truly defeated - Blueprint Newspapers Limited
article.articleSummary: Leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania parasites and transmitted by infected female sandflies, remains endemic in more than 90 countries. Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) causes 600,000–1,000,000 new cases yearly, though underreporting is common. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL) mainly affects the nose, mouth and throat, with most cases in Bolivia, Brazil, Ethiopia and Peru. Visceral leishmaniasis (VL, kala-azar) is fatal if untreated and presents with fever, weight loss and hepatosplenomegaly; VL is most common in Brazil, East Africa and India. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) can follow VL and poses a growing threat in HIV-positive patients, with high relapse and mortality. Risk factors include poverty, malnutrition, migration, housing conditions, and climate change. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with parasitological or rapid tests; treatment uses amphotericin B and pentavalent antimonials. No vaccine exists; prevention emphasizes early detection, vector control, community engagement, and managing animal reservoirs. South-East Asia aims to reduce VL to <1 case per 10,000 by 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Allergies, cough, and viral infections: dengue and typhoid are also making their presence felt—learn how to protect yourself.
article.articleSummary: During Diwali cleaning in Gwalior, rising dust levels can trigger allergies and respiratory symptoms, so wearing masks is advised. With changing season, viral fever is seen, and mosquito-borne diseases are a concern, notably dengue and typhoid, while malaria cases appear relatively lower. Do not ignore fever lasting three to four days; seek medical evaluation, as dengue can cause low platelets and weakness. In addition, viral fever is being observed alongside typhoid in the current period. Prevent mosquitoes by eliminating any standing water around the home, including water tanks, coolers, flower pots, and other receptacles; clean regularly. Use wet cloths instead of dry brooms to reduce dust. Teach children good hand hygiene. Do not self-medicate with antibiotics or other drugs without a doctor’s advice. The doctor emphasizes caution as the key to safe Diwali celebrations.

article.articleHeadline: The Odisha Social Worker Who Transformed Tribal Lives and Eradicated a Neglected Disease - The Logical Indian
article.articleSummary: Shanti Devi, an Odisha social worker born 18 April 1934 in Balasore, devoted nearly six decades to tribal communities, education and health, moving to Koraput and later establishing an ashram at Gobarapalli and founding Seva Samaj in Gunupur (1964). Guided by Gandhian principles and Vinoba Bhave’s Bhoodan ethos, she promoted education for tribal girls, welfare for destitute women and children, and peace in Maoist-affected Odisha. In Sankhalapadar village, where Yaws was endemic, she and nine colleagues helped treat more than 4,000 people, contributing to the eradication of Yaws from the village. She also established an ashram for people affected by leprosy in Jabarguda, Rayagada district. Devi received the Jamnalal Bajaj Award (1994) and the Padma Shri (2021), presented by President Ram Nath Kovind at Rashtrapati Bhavan on 9 November 2021. She died on 16 January 2022, aged 87.

article.articleHeadline: Pune highrises, not slums, emerge as mosquito breeding grounds for dengue, finds joint survey by Pune Municipal Corporation and state health department
article.articleSummary: Dengue-carrying mosquitoes in Pune are primarily breeding in housing societies and highrise complexes rather than slums, a joint Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) and state health department survey conducted in the third week of Oct 2026 found. Stagnant water in household containers, air-conditioner trays, planters and other domestic spots is driving the outbreak, with wards housing dense high-rise buildings and active construction reporting more dengue patients. Slum surveys in Ramtekdi and Wadgaonsheri-Vaiduwadi recorded only two larvae-containing containers among roughly 160 homes, while areas like Aundh-Baner, Nagar Road-Wagholi, Yerawada-Wadgaonsheri and Kothrud showed higher case loads. Highest counts Jan-Oct 21: Aundh-Baner 280; Nagar Road-Wagholi 267; Yerawada-Wadgaonsheri 201; Kothrud 171. Housing societies have hampered surveillance, prompting notices or corporator interventions to gain access. Pre-monsoon vector-control drives in slums aided containment; current focus is on high-rise and redevelopment sites.

article.articleHeadline: Even though dengue is under control, the number of dengue infections rose during Puja week.
article.articleSummary: During Puja week in South 24 Parganas district, West Bengal, dengue infections rose after a period of control. Over seven festival days, 15 new cases were recorded, with the weekly counts moving from 96 (39th week) to 67 (41st week), then 82 (42nd week). By the end of the 42nd week, total district cases reached 796, roughly 300 of them in the Bhangar blocks. Rajpur-Sonarpur Municipality saw a notable spike after seven weeks of near-zero transmission, recording 13 cases in one week, especially in Wards 10 and 35. Officials cited festival-time lapses in surveillance and sanitation—uncollected waste, inadequately cleared drains, and stagnant water—as contributing factors. The outbreak remains under control with ongoing monitoring across areas, and no deaths were reported in the article.

article.articleHeadline: Between 1347 and 1353, the Black Death killed 100 million people: now, DNA has revealed what happened right after.
article.articleSummary: Genetic analysis published in PNAS shows how Yersinia pestis reemerged after the Black Death (1347–1353), potentially killing up to 200 million people across Eurasia and North Africa and reducing Europe's population by up to 50%. The study sequenced 26 pathogen genomes from 11 sites in Estonia, Russia, England, the Netherlands, and Switzerland, combining ancient DNA with radiocarbon dating to refine dates for 75 samples and link them to specific outbreaks recorded by chroniclers. From 1450–1500, the bacterium diversified into three major lineages coinciding with the Great Drought of the Renaissance, a climate-driven wave of rodent movements. Repeated introductions into Estonia affected urban and rural settings. War-related troop movements and refugees—illustrated by campaigns such as the Thirty Years’ War, the Great Northern War, and the 1710 Tallinn siege—sped transmission. These historical insights aid modern epidemiology of zoonoses, though dating challenges remain.

article.articleHeadline: Health Thailand Issues Soil Fever Warning After 136 Deaths
article.articleSummary: Melioidosis (soil fever) in Thailand has claimed 136 deaths and more than 3,100 infections this year, with heavy monsoon rainfall and floodwaters elevating exposure among rural farming communities. Northeastern provinces including Mukdahan, Bueng Kan, and Ubon Ratchathani report rising cases as authorities monitor hospitals nationwide. Burkholderia pseudomallei, present in damp soil and rural waterways, infects agricultural workers when contaminated water enters wounds or they inhale dust during storms. Early symptoms mimic common respiratory illnesses; patients develop sudden high fever, persistent cough, joint stiffness, and localized skin abscesses about 4–9 days after exposure. Definitive detection requires targeted laboratory blood cultures; untreated infections can rapidly progress to septic shock and organ failure. High-risk groups include farmers, adults over 50, and individuals with diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Preventive measures: wear waterproof boots/gloves, boil drinking water, cleanse wounds; call 1422 and seek urgent care if fever develops.

article.articleHeadline: UST health experts warn of disease resurgence amid low immunization coverage
article.articleSummary: UST health experts warn that low childhood immunization could trigger measles (tigdas) and rubella (tigdas-hangin) outbreaks in the Philippines. DOH records show 80,702 children fully immunized in June 2026 (3.63% of the projected infant population), down from May and far below the 7.92% monthly target. January–June cumulative coverage reached 25.63% for 2.22 million infants, versus a 95% annual target. From Jan 4–Sept 12, 68% of measles and 26% of rubella cases involved unvaccinated individuals, highlighting persistent vaccine hesitancy. Unvaccinated people face higher risk of severe illness; herd immunity could break down, risking outbreaks that strain health services. Measles can cause pneumonia or encephalitis; rubella endangers pregnancy, risking stillbirth or miscarriage. The routine schedule includes birth hepatitis B and BCG, and infancy measles vaccines; side effects are usually mild, severe allergies rare. WHO/UNICEF emphasize immunization to prevent deaths.

article.articleHeadline: Town requires meat inspection amid suspected swine fever case
article.articleSummary: Suspected African swine fever (ASF) case in a neighboring town prompts Santander, Cebu to tighten pig movement controls and require pre-slaughter inspection, even for meat for personal consumption. An Oct. 30, 2026 advisory implements border controls to prevent entry and spread of swine diseases. Measures follow the ASF outbreak in Ginatilan, where the outbreak was declared contained on Oct. 20 after 60 blood samples from pigs in 12 barangays tested negative. Ginatilan had ASF detected in September, triggering movement restrictions, slaughter bans and border controls. Gov. Baricuatro issued Executive Order 55 (Oct. 26) allowing entry of live hogs only if intended for immediate slaughter at National Meat Inspection Service-accredited facilities, with complete documents and negative RT-PCR results; shipments must go to NMIS-accredited slaughterhouses and may be confiscated if incomplete or misdirected. ASF does not infect humans, but causes high pig mortality; no secondary infections reported.

article.articleHeadline: Fake albumin, rabies serum found in Davao City
article.articleSummary: Two counterfeit drug batches were collected in Davao City: Albumin (Human) USP 25% Albuminar-25, 50 mL IV solution, Lot Nos. NGC826348 and PRT279082; and Anti-Rabies Serum (Equine) Equirab 200 IU/mL, 5 mL vial, Lot A06825016. Across the Davao Region, five counterfeit products from four establishments have tested positive, with more samples pending. FDA advisories warn against counterfeit Albuminar (CSL Behring no longer manufactures Albuminar; AlbuRx 25% 50 mL is the authorized product; last Albuminar batch expired Sept 2022) and against counterfeit Equirab (Lot A06825016; exp March 2027). Rabies immunoglobulin is essential after severe exposures, and counterfeit products pose serious health risks. Price red flags include anti-rabies vaccines offered around P600 instead of over P1,000. Consumers are urged to buy only FDA-licensed drug stores, check the FDA portal, and report suspected fakes via the FDA website. DOH/FDA briefing occurred Oct 30, 2026, ahead of counterfeit medicines week.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana Health Service Confirms Cholera Outbreak In Ashanti Region
article.articleSummary: As of 1 November 2026, cholera outbreak confirmed in Ghana's Ashanti Region, with 47 suspected cases across Kumasi Metropolis, Asokwa and Oforikrom; 12 laboratory-confirmed positives at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital. First case reported May 6, 2026, a 32-year-old trader from Asafo Market with severe diarrhea and vomiting. Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, spreads via contaminated food or water; common symptoms include watery stools, vomiting, dehydration, and weakness. Health authorities activated emergency response teams and intensified surveillance region-wide. Samples were tested at KATH; officials collaboration with the Ministry of Health, Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly, and National Commission for Civic Education to educate the public on prevention. Government released funds and medical supplies; KMA disinfected markets, public toilets, and drainage; enforcement of sanitation bye-laws. Health workers are treating patients with oral rehydration salts; public advised to practice handwashing, safe water, hot cooked food. Reports updated via GNA and credible media.

article.articleHeadline: Yellow fever outbreak has been curtailed after four confirmed cases - GHS
article.articleSummary: Ghana Health Service (GHS) says the yellow fever outbreak has been curtailed after four laboratory-confirmed cases recorded between September and the first half of October. The confirmed cases were detected in Sissala West, Wa West, and the communities of Etu and Nadowli-Kaleo. Cases were confirmed through laboratory testing in Dakar, Senegal, guiding containment via a vaccination campaign. The four cases are officially confirmed, with vaccination exercises ongoing as part of the response. Investigations are underway to determine whether deaths in affected communities were due to yellow fever, amid speculation. Health authorities also cautioned health workers against public announcements of suspected outbreaks without authorization and laboratory confirmation, noting premature disclosures can create fear and complicate corrections. As of 1 November 2026, the outbreak has been curtailed.
